newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Swiss banks to list Holocaust assets soon - envoy.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks to list Holocaust assets soon - envoy.

text.p: A Swiss official said after meeting Jewish survivors of the Nazi Holocaust on Friday that Swiss banks would this summer unveil "all information" on unclaimed accounts of Holocaust victims.

"This summer the Swiss banks are releasing all information they have concerning dormant accounts," Ambassador Thomas Borer, head of a Swiss Foreign Ministry task force untangling Swiss World War Two business dealings with the Nazis, told Reuters.

Allegations that Switzerland cynically profited from its wartime ties with Germany through purchases of Nazi gold - some looted from the teeth of Holocaust victims - and that Swiss banks hoarded victims' unclaimed assets have thrust the neutral republic into a harsh international spotlight.
The Swiss have lifted bank secrecy for an independent panel hunting for unclaimed accounts and another writing a broad history of the country's wartime role as a financial centre.
Switzerland has set up a $185 million Holocaust memorial fund with donations from banks and businesses and has proposed a $4.7 billion "Solidarity Foundation" to help victims of human rights abuses.
Borer on Friday met Holocaust victims in Israel, which has the world's largest survivor population of 300,000.

The executive director of Amcha, an Israeli centre which supports Holocaust victims, urged Borer not to delay aiding elderly survivors until the Swiss panels had completed their lengthy investigations.
"My concern and the concern of Amcha is when we talk about elderly survivors it has to be done yesterday and not tomorrow," John Lemberger told Reuters.
"The feeling of all survivors is that restitution is too little too late, whether its Germany in the 50s and 60s or Switzerland in the 90s."
Six million Jews were killed by Nazi Germany.
Borer said he understood the need for speed and would press for quick disbursal of the memorial fund.
"We are talking about weeks to start paying attention to Holocaust survivors because we see they are old and we see they are needy. The money is there. We need to go," Borer said.

He added that Eastern European survivors should also be a priority: "I heard a lot about the needy victims in Eastern Europe, the 'double victims' as they are called who never got anything from anyone."
Borer said his meeting was very moving and that he was touched by the stories of two survivors who had escaped Germany across the Alps and been granted refuge in Switzerland.
"This is something that I don't hear much of these days."
Borer on Wednesday defended his country's sales of millions of dollars of arms to Adolf Hitler's military during the war, saying Switzerland was too small to resist Nazi Germany.

Swiss diplomatic archives released on Wednesday showed that Switzerland exported some 900 million Swiss francs worth of arms during the war, two-thirds of which was sold to the Nazis. Documents also showed the Swiss central bank may have known it was buying looted Nazi gold.
